mcqs.question: When reconstructing a tree from preorder and inorder sequences, what specific information does the inorder sequence provide that preorder alone lacks?
options: The exact value of the root node
The number of nodes in the entire tree
Which elements belong to the left subtree versus the right subtree, since inorder places the root between them
The height of the reconstructed tree
mcqs.explanation: Preorder already tells you the root (it's always first), but says nothing about how many of the remaining elements belong to each subtree; locating the root's value within inorder reveals exactly that split, since everything to its left in inorder is the left subtree and everything to its right is the right subtree. Total node count and tree height aren't the missing pieces here — the split boundary is.

mcqs.question: When reconstructing a tree from postorder and inorder, where is the root found, and how does the construction direction differ from preorder+inorder?
options: The root is the first element of postorder, identical to preorder's rule
The root is the last element of postorder, and construction proceeds by consuming postorder from the end, processing the right subtree before the left
The root must be found by searching postorder for the smallest value
Postorder and inorder cannot be used together to reconstruct a tree
mcqs.explanation: Postorder visits the node after both its subtrees, so the root is always the last element — the mirror of preorder's rule — and correctly consuming the array means working backward from that end, which naturally processes the right subtree first since it's the last one visited before the root. Root position isn't determined by value magnitude, and postorder+inorder is a fully valid, commonly used reconstruction pair.

mcqs.question: Why can't preorder and postorder alone (without inorder) uniquely reconstruct an arbitrary binary tree?
options: For a node with exactly one child, neither sequence reveals whether that child is the left or right child — both possibilities produce identical preorder and postorder sequences
Preorder and postorder sequences always have different lengths, making comparison impossible
This is only a problem for trees with more than 100 nodes
Preorder and postorder can only be used with balanced trees
mcqs.explanation: The ambiguity is specific to single-child nodes: since neither traversal places the node between its children the way inorder does, there's no way to distinguish 'this child is on the left' from 'this child is on the right' when only one exists — both configurations yield the same two sequences. This has nothing to do with sequence length mismatches, tree size thresholds, or balance — full binary trees (0-or-2 children only) are actually the exception where this ambiguity doesn't arise.

mcqs.question: Why can level-order-with-nulls serialization produce a much larger output than preorder-with-nulls for a heavily skewed tree?
options: Level-order serialization is only valid for complete trees

Every level must include null markers for both children of every real node lacking a full set of children, which accumulates heavily on skewed shapes, unlike preorder's nulls which are bounded more tightly by actual node count
Preorder serialization cannot represent skewed trees at all
Level-order serialization always produces exactly double the preorder output regardless of tree shape
mcqs.explanation: A skewed tree has many nodes with only one real child, and level-order marking requires an explicit null for every missing child at every level until a level goes fully empty — this compounds on skewed shapes in a way preorder's structure doesn't. Level-order serialization works for any tree shape, not just complete ones, preorder handles skewed trees fine, and the size difference isn't a fixed ratio — it depends entirely on the tree's specific shape.

mcqs.question: The standard preorder+inorder reconstruction uses a value-to-index map for O(1) lookups. Why does this break down if the tree contains duplicate values?
options: It doesn't break down — the map still works correctly with duplicates

A value-to-index map can only store one index per value, discarding information about earlier occurrences, and duplicate values can make the reconstruction genuinely ambiguous regardless of the map implementation
Duplicate values only cause a problem if the tree has more than one root
The map approach fails only for trees taller than the number of distinct values
mcqs.explanation: A dictionary keyed by value inherently keeps just one index per key, silently losing earlier occurrences when duplicates exist — but the deeper issue is structural, not just an implementation detail: with genuine duplicate values, multiple distinct trees can produce the identical preorder/inorder pair, so no indexing fix restores a unique answer. This isn't about multiple roots (a tree has exactly one) or tree height relative to distinct value count — it's a fundamental ambiguity introduced by non-unique values.
